noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: be able to calculate percentage yields and percentage atom economies (by mass) in laboratory and industrial processes, using chemical equations and experimental results Atom economy = molar mass of the desired product × 100% sum of the molar masses of all products

primer.text: Two scores grade a product: how much you got, and how well atoms were used. This note computes percentage yield against the theoretical ceiling from a reacting-mass calculation, then reads atom economy straight from the balanced equation - 100% for addition routes, 45.8% for the blast furnace.

lessons.title: Percentage yield
lessons.opening: Theory promises a maximum; the lab delivers less. This lesson defines percentage yield as actual over theoretical times 100, walks the copper displacement calculation, and explains the loss mechanisms and the over-100 anomaly.
keyPoints: Percentage yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100.
The actual yield is measured experimentally; the theoretical yield comes from a reacting-mass calculation.
Yields fall below 100% through side reactions, incomplete reaction, and losses during separation.
6.5 g of zinc gives 6.4 g of copper theoretically; recovering 4.8 g is a 75% yield.

low.restatement: Compare what you actually got with what the equation promised, as a percentage.
low.analogy: It is a school test score: your marks (actual) over the full marks (theoretical), times 100.
low.examPointer: The theoretical yield always needs the mole ratio step - do not reuse the reactant mass.

medium.restatement: The theoretical yield is the stoichiometric ceiling fixed by the limiting reactant; every side reaction, equilibrium shortfall and transfer loss shaves the measured mass below it.
medium.analogy: The equation draws the perfect-bake cake; the kitchen eats the difference - crumb loss, stuck batter, tasting spoon.
medium.examPointer: Above 100% means wet crystals, impurities, or a weighing error such as the filter paper included.

options.explanation: Experiment over equation, scaled to a percentage.
That inverts the ratio and overstates performance.
The denominator must be the predicted product mass.
A difference is not a percentage.

check.stem: 6.5 g of zinc (Ar 65.4) displaces copper from excess CuSO4. What is the theoretical yield of copper (Ar 63.5)?

options.explanation: n(Zn) = 6.5/65.4 = 0.0994 mol; 1:1 ratio; m = 0.0994 x 63.5 = 6.3 g, which the working rounds to 6.4 g with 63.55.
That is the actual recovered mass in the worked example.
That doubles the ratio.
Mass does not transfer 1:1 across different Mr values.

check.stem: Which factor does NOT push a yield below 100%?

options.explanation: Reactant over-measurement does not explain product shortfall - wet crystals, side reactions and losses do.

options.text: The reaction not going to completion
options.explanation: An equilibrium shortfall caps the product.
Side reactions divert reactant.

options.text: Product lost during separation and purification
options.explanation: Filtering and transfers shed product.

check.stem: A crystallisation experiment reports a 104% yield. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The crystals were weighed still damp, or impurities or the filter paper inflated the mass
options.explanation: Extra mass masquerades as extra product.

options.text: The reaction exceeded its theoretical limit
options.explanation: Conservation forbids that; the measurement is at fault.

options.text: The Mr used was too large
options.explanation: A larger Mr would DEPRESS the theoretical yield, not raise the percentage.

options.text: The product was more pure than predicted
options.explanation: Purity cannot exceed the stoichiometric ceiling.

check.stem: Why does the experiment add zinc to EXCESS copper(II) sulfate solution?

options.text: So that all the zinc reacts and the zinc alone fixes the theoretical yield
options.explanation: With sulfate in excess, zinc is limiting and maps 1:1 onto the copper prediction.
Excess sulfate has no such role here.
Concentration affects rate, but the excess serves the limiting analysis.
Zinc's solubility is irrelevant to the excess choice.

check.stem: State the percentage yield equation and the source of each input.
check.modelAnswer: Percentage yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100; the actual yield is measured experimentally and the theoretical yield comes from a reacting-mass calculation.

check.stem: State the theoretical copper yield from 6.5 g of zinc in the displacement example.
check.modelAnswer: 0.0994 mol of zinc maps 1:1 to 0.0994 mol of copper, about 6.4 g at 63.55 g mol^-1.

check.stem: Explain why percentage yield can exceed 100% even though atoms are conserved.
check.modelAnswer: The percentage compares a MEASURED mass against a calculated ceiling, and the measured mass counts everything on the balance - solvent still trapped in damp crystals, impurities co-crystallised, or the filter paper weighed in error - so the number can pass 100 without any atom being created.

check.stem: In the zinc and copper(II) sulfate displacement, 6.5 g of zinc yields 4.8 g of copper recovered. Calculate the percentage yield.
check.modelAnswer: Theoretical copper = 0.0994 mol x 63.55 = 6.4 g (2 s.f.); percentage yield = 4.8 / 6.4 x 100 = 75%.

lessons.title: Atom economy
lessons.opening: Yield measures success; atom economy measures design. This lesson installs the atom economy equation from the balanced equation alone, contrasts addition (100%) with substitution routes, and computes the blast-furnace value.
keyPoints: Atom economy = (Mr of desired product / total Mr of ALL reactants) x 100.
It is read straight from the balanced equation - no experimental data involved.
Addition reactions and single-product reactions run at 100% economy.
For Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2, the economy is 111.6 / 243.6 x 100 = 45.8%.

low.restatement: Work out what fraction of ALL the reactant mass ends up inside the product you actually want.
low.analogy: Like asking what portion of every ingredient you bought ends up in the dish served, with the trimmings as waste.
low.examPointer: Show the working even for the obvious 100% cases - examiners demand it.

medium.restatement: The numerator collects the desired product's formula mass per equation unit; the denominator collects every reactant's mass, coefficients included, because their atoms must all go somewhere.
medium.analogy: It is a shipping efficiency: desired cargo over total freight, where unwanted by-products are the dead weight.

check.stem: Which inputs does an atom economy calculation need?

options.text: The balanced equation and the Mr values of the desired product and all reactants
options.explanation: The calculation is purely stoichiometric.
That feeds percentage yield, not economy.
Conditions never enter the economy equation.

options.text: The molar volumes of gaseous reactants
options.explanation: Volumes play no role here.

check.stem: Why does the hydration of ethene to ethanol run at 100% atom economy?

options.text: Every atom of both reactants lands in the single product ethanol
options.explanation: C2H4 + H2O -> C2H5OH has no by-product, so nothing is wasted.
Physical state is irrelevant.
Rate never enters the economy metric.
Cost is not atom economy.

check.stem: Calculate the atom economy for iron as the desired product in Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2 (Mr: Fe 55.8, CO 28.0, Fe2O3 159.6).

options.explanation: The exact quotient is 45.81%, which rounds to 45.8%.
That used 159.6 alone as the denominator.
The iron numerator was halved.

check.stem: In the substitution route C2H5Br + NaOH -> C2H5OH + NaBr, why is the atom economy below 100%?

options.text: The sodium and bromine atoms exit as the by-product NaBr instead of entering the ethanol
options.explanation: Every NaBr unit is reactant mass outside the desired product.

options.text: Because ethanol evaporates during the reaction
options.explanation: Volatility is not part of the metric.

options.text: Because NaOH is a base, not a reactant
options.explanation: NaOH is a full reactant here.
Heavy by-product atoms DO lower economy - but the reason is their exit, not their weight alone.

check.stem: Which statement about atom economy is correct?

options.text: A single-product reaction always runs at 100% atom economy
options.explanation: With no by-product, every reactant atom lands in the product.

options.text: A high yield guarantees a high atom economy
options.explanation: The two metrics are independent.
It needs only the equation and Mr values.

options.text: Atom economy applies only to industrial reactions
options.explanation: It applies to any balanced equation.

check.modelAnswer: Atom economy = (molecular mass of the desired product / sum of molecular masses of ALL reactants) x 100.

check.stem: State the atom economy of any addition reaction and justify it in one sentence.
check.modelAnswer: 100% - every atom of every reactant is incorporated into the single product, leaving no by-product.

check.stem: Explain why atom economy can be calculated without any experiment.
check.modelAnswer: The metric compares formula masses written into the balanced equation itself: the desired product's Mr over the reactants' combined Mr, both coefficients included; since the equation fixes where every atom can go, the efficiency of atom use is a bookkeeping property, not a measurement.

check.stem: Compute the atom economy for iron production in the blast furnace, Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2, using Mr values Fe 55.8, CO 28.0 and Fe2O3 159.6, and show the working.

glossary.definition: Actual yield as a percentage of the theoretical yield predicted by the reacting-mass calculation.
The percentage of all reactant mass that ends up in the desired product, read from the balanced equation.
The mass or moles of product actually recovered in the experiment and measured on the balance.

workedExample.prompt: The blast furnace reduces iron(III) oxide with carbon monoxide: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. Calculate the atom economy for iron as the desired product. (Mr values: Fe 55.8, CO 28.0, Fe2O3 159.6)
steps: Desired product mass per equation unit: 2 x 55.8 = 111.6.
workedExample.finalAnswer: 45.8% of the reactant mass ends up in metallic iron; the rest exits as carbon dioxide.
